document.title: Motion for Leave to File Limited Answer, and Limited Answer, of East Kentucky Power Cooperative, Inc. in support of Protest filed by American Electric Power…

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.  
 
) 
 
Docket No. ER26-3380-000 
 
MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE LIMITED ANSWER, 
AND LIMITED ANSWER, OF 
EAST KENTUCKY POWER COOPERATIVE, INC. 
Pursuant to Rule 212 and 213 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 East 
Kentucky Power Cooperative, Inc. (“EKPC”) moves for leave to answer and answers in support 
of the protests of American Electric Power Service Corporation (“AEP”),2 Indicated PJM 
Transmission Owners (“Indicated TOs”),3 and PPL Electric Utilities Corporation4 (“PPL Electric” 
together with AEP and Indicated TOs, “RBP Protestors”) in the above-captioned proceeding. As 
explained further below, EKPC supports the RBP Protestors with respect to the arguments made 
concerning PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) proposed treatment of Reliability Backstop 
Procurement (“RBP”) commitments in the event that a Transmission Owner (“TO”) exits from 
PJM during the RBP commitment period. 
I. 
MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER 
Rule 213(a)(2) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure generally prohibits 
answers to answers or protests unless otherwise ordered by the decisional authority. Here, good 
cause justifies the Commission’s granting this motion and accepting this Limited Answer because 
 
1 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 385.213 (2026). 
2 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-3380-000, “Limited Protest of American Electric Power Service 
Corporation” (filed Apr. 3, 2026) (“AEP Protest”). 
3 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-3380-000, “Protest of the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners” 
(filed Aug. 21, 2026) (“Indicated TOs Protest”). 
4 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-3380-000, “Motion for to Intervene, Limited Protest, and Request 
for Clarification of PPL Electric Utilities Corporation” (filed Aug. 21, 2026) (“PPL Electric Protest”).

2 
it provides information that may assist the Commission in its decision-making process.5 For these 
reasons, the Commission should accept this Limited Answer. 
II. 
LIMITED ANSWER 
This proceeding concerns PJM’s July 31, 2026 filing6 proposing revisions to the PJM Open 
Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) and Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load Serving 
Entities (“RAA”) to establish the RBP to address previously identified resource adequacy 
challenges that have arisen as a result of insufficient capacity commitments in the 2027/2028 and 
2028/2029 Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”) Capacity Market Auctions (“RBP Proposal”). 
EKPC filed a protest to PJM’s RBP Proposal.7 
As explained in the RBP Protests, PJM proposed new rules that “set forth the 
responsibilities of various parties in the event a Transmission Owner exits from PJM”8 (“TO Exit 
Provisions”) and that would impose new financial obligations on any TO that exits PJM during 
the fifteen-year term of the RBP commitment.9 For example, the TO Exit Provisions would require 
an exiting TO with net load to pay, on an accelerated basis, all future RBP charges it would have 
owed, or enter into a binding agreement with the owners of the RBP resources to preserve the RBP 
commitments.10 Or, if the exiting TO leaves with net generation, the TO must ensure that the RBP-
 
5 See, e.g., PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 189 FERC ¶ 61,110, P 22 (2024) (accepting answers to protests and answers 
because they assisted the Commission in its decision-making process); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 181 FERC ¶ 
61,162, P 29 (2022). Potomac-Appalachian Transmission Highline, LLC, 140 FERC ¶ 61,229, P 102 (2012) 
(accepting answer to an answer because it provided material evidence that corrected the record and informed the 
Commission’s decision-making process); N.E. Utils. Servs. Co. v. NRG Energy, Inc., 101 FERC ¶ 61,327, P 17 
(2002) (accepting answer to an answer because it helped clarify issues in the proceeding). 
6 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-3380-000, “Reliability Backstop Procurement to Address Resource 
Adequacy Concerns Stemming from Large Loads” (filed July 31, 2026) (“PJM RBP Filing”). 
7 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-3380-000, “Protest of East Kentucky Power Cooperative, Inc.” (filed 
Aug. 21, 2026) (“EKPC Protest”). 
8 PJM RBP Filing at 90. 
9 See Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD, § 18.7. 
10 PJM RBP Filing at 94-95.

3 
contracted generation continues to serve PJM through a pseudo-tie, pay the remaining RBP 
obligations in full on an accelerated basis, or execute an agreement to maintain the RBP 
commitments, essentially stepping into PJM’s role with respect to RBP.11 
As PJM did not place any locational limitations on capacity resources offering into the 
RBP, it is possible that selected resources could locate within EKPC’s service territory even though 
PJM is not intending to solicit RBP resources to serve EKPC load. EKPC has not submitted any 
Large Load Adjustments to PJM, which PJM assumes to be in the RBP Procurement Target, and 
does not anticipate receiving a direct assignment of RBP Costs. As a result, potentially allocating 
to EKPC any costs related to RBP selected resources should, at some point over the next 15 years, 
EKPC contemplate exit from PJM is completely divorced from cost causation and not just and 
reasonable. 
Having been introduced at the very end of the stakeholder process, PJM’s TO Exit 
Provisions were not discussed among stakeholders. Understandably PJM desires clear and 
enforceable commitments; however, its proposal goes too far and imposes obligations on exiting 
TOs unbounded by the cost causation principle. As a result, it should be rejected. EKPC agrees 
with the arguments set forth by AEP, the Indicated TOs, and PPL Electric: PJM’s proposal unfairly 
expands the negotiated terms of exit embedded in the Consolidated Transmission Owner’s 
Agreement (“CTOA”), Operating Agreement (“OA”), and RAA.12 Therefore, any imposition of 
 
11 PJM RBP Filing at 92-94. 
12 Each TO has a contractual right to leave a Regional Transmission Organization (“RTO”), and the Commission, 
under its Federal Power Act (“FPA”) section 205 authority, ensures that the departing utility satisfies its “contractual 
obligations” applicable to it under its RTO’s governing documents upon withdrawal. See AEP Protest at 21. In PJM’s 
case, these requirements are clear. Section 3.4 of the CTOA requires payment of Regional Transmission Expansion 
Plan fees; however, the CTOA does not require an exit fee. See AEP Protest at 25. Section 5.1.1 of the RAA requires 
payment of capacity PJM acquired on the Load Serving Entity’s (“LSE”) behalf, up to and including the last capacity 
auction in which the LSE’s load forecast was included. See id. at 26. And new provision to RAA – Section 7.2A 
requires payment of all section 202(c) charges allocated to it. See id.

4 
an exit fee that obligates departing load to pay for charges that are unrelated to its fair allocation 
of RBP commitments because they exceed or are not based not on the RBP Charges allocated to 
an Electric Distributor zone/area is not just and reasonable. 
A. The TO Exit Provisions Violate the Cost Causation Principle. 
EKPC agrees with the RBP Protestors that the TO Exit Provisions violate the cost causation 
principle. The Commission’s cost causation principle requires that “all approved rates reflect to 
some degree the costs actually caused by the customer who must pay them,” in order to be found 
just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential under FPA section 205.13 Here, 
the TO Exit Provisions impose costs that do not align with an exiting TO’s obligations under the 
RBP Proposal.14 
In its Protest, AEP highlights the disconnect between the potential financial obligations an 
exiting TO may be responsible for relative to the RBP Charges it would pay if it remained in PJM, 
assuming the Commission accepted the RBP Proposal cost allocation methodology and the costs 
that would be imposed if it exited PJM.15 The exit fee requires the TO to take on costs driven by 
“where PJM happens to procure or locate new RBP resources.”16 EKPC echoes AEP’s concerns 
that if PJM acquired new RBP resources in the exiting TO’s zone, the exiting TO would be required 
to pay for such RBP resources regardless of whether such RBP resources are tied to that TO.17 To 
require TOs to pay more than their obligation would be inconsistent with the Commission’s cost 
 
13 KN Energy, Inc. v. FERC, 968 F.2d 1295, 1300 (D.C. Cir. 1992). 
14 In its Protest, EKPC raised concerns regarding the cost allocation and rate impact of the RBP Proposal. See EKPC 
Protest at 15-21 (the RBP Proposal is unjust and unreasonable because the resulting rate impact is uncertain) and 28-
31 (PJM’s proposals with respect to decrementing and use of offsets are unjust and unreasonable because they ignore 
the Commission’s cost causation principles). 
15 AEP Protest at 17-20. 
16 AEP Protest at 11. 
17 AEP Protest at 18.

5 
causation policy. PJM cannot penalize a TO for exercising its contractual rights to leave PJM by 
imposing an exit fee greater than the RBP Charges that it would otherwise be allocated.18 
Further, EKPC agrees with the Indicated TOs that the TO Exit Provisions violate cost 
causation principles “by allocating generation- and capacity-related costs to TOs, which neither 
caused nor will benefit from these costs.”19 An exiting TO should not be responsible for the RBP 
commitments of generation resources and load within its zone where such costs cannot be 
construed as transmission-related costs properly allocated to the TO. The costs of procuring 
generation capacity under the RBP Proposal are driven by Load Serving Entities (“LSEs”) and 
their customers, not TOs. 
B. The TO Exit Provisions Lack the Required Clarity and Specificity to be 
Found Just and Reasonable. 
 
As proposed, the TO Exit Provisions lack the clarity and specificity required for a TO to 
determine its obligations upon withdrawal from PJM. EKPC agrees with PPL Electric that any exit 
provision should not run afoul of the Commission’s requirement that rates be “clear and 
specifically set forth.”20 PPL Electric identifies language, such as “all costs” and “all forward 
obligations,” that exemplifies the financial uncertainty created by the TO Exit Provisions.21 The 
proposal does not include definitions for such costs nor include a limiting principle associated with 
the costs sufficient to provide certainty for the exiting TO. 
Similarly, EKPC agrees with AEP that any RBP exit provisions must provide “a 
transparent and reasonably calculable measure of the financial consequences of withdrawal” in 
 
18 AEP Protest at 18. 
19 Indicated TOs Protest at 10. 
20 PPL Electric Protest at 11 (citing 18 C.F.R. § 35.1(a)). 
21 PPL Electric Protest at 11.

6 
order to make informed decisions.22 As explained in EKPC’s Protest, a rate that is impermissibly 
vague such that customers cannot determine their cost burden is unjust and unreasonable.23 The 
TO Exit Provisions do not have sufficient specificity to allow a TO to calculate the costs it will 
face should it choose to leave PJM, and therefore the Commission should find that they are not 
just and reasonable. 
Moreover, any exit obligation related to the RBP Proposal should be limited to that which 
is necessary to prevent RBP charges from being shifted to remaining load.24 Should the 
Commission accept PJM’s RBP Proposal,25 EKPC urges the Commission to be clear that its 
determination in this proceeding is confined to the specific proposed Tariff language governing 
RBP Charges and does not disturb the Commission’s existing precedent regarding other PJM 
contractual exit commitments.26 Notwithstanding that PJM’s RBP Proposal makes it challenging 
to determine the RBP Charges with certainty,27 EKPC concurs with AEP’s request that the 
Commission should “expressly reaffirm that any expansion of a Transmission Owner’s 
responsibility for charges upon withdrawal accepted in this proceeding is limited to RBP charges 
and does not otherwise expand to a departing TO’s obligations under the TO Agreement, RAA, or 
PJM Tariff.”28 
 
22 AEP Protest at 19-20. See also Tri-State Generation & Transmission Ass’n, 175 FERC ¶ 61,229, P 12 (2021) 
(finding the proposed Contract Termination Payment (“CTP”) to be “impermissibly vague because it lack[ed] detailed 
procedures governing when and how a utility member may obtain a CTP methodology calculation” and “utility 
members [could not] estimate their own CTP payments or reasonably predict the impacts of a membership 
withdrawal” since the calculation relied on proprietary information). 
23 EKPC Protest at 15-16. 
24 See AEP Protest at 27. 
25 As noted, EKPC protested the PJM RBP Filing and requested that the Commission reject the RBP Proposal. 
26 AEP Protest at 27. 
27 See EKPC Protest at 15. 
28 AEP Protest at 28.

7 
C. The TO Exit Provisions “Unnecessarily Constrain Future Decision-Making.” 
PJM concedes that a TO withdrawing is a “remote” possibility yet proposes rigid 
obligations that very likely would need to be revisited if a TO sought to withdraw over the 15-year 
RBP commitment period. EKPC agrees with PPL Electric that the proposed TO Exit Provisions 
would “unnecessarily constrain” the parties involved in effectuating a TO’s withdrawal from PJM, 
including the Commission and state regulatory authorities.29 Any withdrawal would require 
extensive negotiations and communications amongst the parties taking into account the specific 
facts and circumstances at that time.30 Additionally, any withdrawal would already need to comply 
with the CTOA provisions, which require Commission authorization of the withdrawal.31 As PPL 
Electric argued, “preemptively mandating how the costs and contractual arrangements of 
generation resources and load within an exiting Transmission Owner’s zone must be treated” is 
not necessary and likely will need to be revisited when the actual, specific circumstances are 
considered.32 Accordingly, EKPC urges the Commission to reject PJM’s proposed TO Exit 
Provisions. 
 
29 PPL Electric Protest at 9-10. 
30 PPL Electric Protest at 9-10. 
31 PPL Electric Protest at 9-10 (citing CTOA, Section 3.2). 
32 PPL Electric Protest at 10 (emphasis in original).

8 
III. 
CONCLUSION 
Wherefore, EKPC respectfully requests that the Commission accept this answer, consider 
the arguments set forth herein, and take such action as requested herein and in the EKPC Protest. 
 
Respectfully submitted,
